1:
Zophar the Naamathite rises for the last time, and the witnesses gather less around the bare formula of the verse than around the temper and the design of the speech it opens. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the tone at once: Zophar retorts with yet greater vehemence than before, assuming a more ornate and elaborate style, and still reiterating the old burden of his party — the speedy doom of the wicked man. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the whole plan of the discourse that follows, in which Zophar details the wretchedness of the wicked and the hypocrite, shows that their rejoicing is short and transitory (vv.1-9), that such a man is punished in his family and his person, stripped of his ill-gotten wealth and made miserable in the midst of affluence, until he dies a violent death and his house is destroyed at the last (v.29).

The reformed John Gill measures the hardness of the reply against the state of the man it answers. Notwithstanding the sad and distressed condition Job was in, notwithstanding his earnest plea for pity, the noble confession of faith he had made, and the grave counsel he had given his friends to cease persecuting him, Zophar — regardless of all these things — starts up and attacks him with as much heat and passion, wrath and anger as ever, harping upon the same string and still representing Job as a wicked man and a hypocrite. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great reads the friends' whole failure at a deeper level: instructed by long habit to good living, they knew how to live well, yet, being untrained to form an exact estimate of God's judgments, they could not believe it possible that any righteous man should be susceptible of ills here below, and hence they imagined that holy man to be wicked whom they saw scourged.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening an exposition that will run to the chapter's end, hears in Zophar a man resolved to condemn Job for a bad man, and much displeased that he should talk so like a good one. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the frame for the speech. A true doctrine — that the triumph of the wicked is short — is seized by a passionate advocate and bent, unjustly, into one more indictment of an innocent sufferer, so that (as Henry will say at the close) never was any doctrine better explained, or worse applied.
2:
The impulse that drives the speech is named in the verse itself, and the witnesses weigh how much of it is thought and how much is heat. The reformed John Gill takes Zophar at his own valuation: his thoughts cause him to answer, or to return and enter the lists once more; the reflections came so thick and fast upon him that out of their abundance his heart constrained him to speak. He is anxious, Gill notes, to have it understood that his answer proceeded from thought — that he did not speak without weighing things, and that what he was about to say was the fruit of close thinking and mature deliberation. He had thought, perhaps, to say no more in the dispute; but, observing what Job had said last, he could not forbear, and returns to the stage to enter the lists once more.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will allow him no such composure. Zophar, he says, is the most inveterate of Job's adversaries — one must really cease to call them friends — who sets no bounds to his invective and outrages every rule of charity; and the only modesty in the whole discourse is the confession of this verse, which Clarke, following Good, renders as a question, "Whither would my tumult transport me? and how far my agitation within me?" The Hebrew, he adds, says plainly "there is sensibility in me" — my feelings provoke me to reply. A man of so bitter a spirit, Clarke remarks, must in general have been very unhappy; and with him Job is, by insinuation, everything base, vile, and hypocritical. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it to the same effect but more soberly: the "therefore" points back to the eagerness that is in him, his spirit stirred within and impelling him to answer.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, labour over the crux of the second clause. Most expositors, they observe, take it as an apology for the vehemence that follows and supply an elliptical "therefore"; but the popular rendering "the storm within me" leans on a sense that Schultens drew from the Arabic — perturbatio animi — which lies too far from Hebrew usage to be trusted. The emendations that would smooth the line they find equally unsupported, so that the clause stands, on their judgment, as an apology wrung from a man who cannot keep silent. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the plain drift: for "this thy severe sentence" Zophar makes haste, speaking sooner than he intended, and, it may be, breaking in upon Job before he had finished his discourse. The witnesses do not divide over the fact of the man's haste; they differ only in how much credit to give his claim that thought, and not mere passion, is its spring.
3:
Zophar names the sting that has roused him and the faculty he claims to answer from, and here a genuine fork opens among the witnesses. "The check of my reproach," the reformed John Gill explains, is the reproof Job had given the friends when he bade them beware of the sword, lest the judgment fall upon themselves; Zophar heard it, could not bear it with patience, and made haste to reply. He took it that Job had reproached him and his friends as hard-hearted persecutors, and that the check was Job's warning of a righteous judgment they could not escape; and this he could not hear with patience. But Gill records a very different construction alongside: some think Zophar here pretends to a divine oracle, as Eliphaz had claimed at the outset of the dispute, so that "the correction of my reproach" means a confutation he has heard from God, with which, being thus divinely furnished, he thought it his duty to answer.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps him on the lower ground. Zophar quotes Job's own words, recalling the complaint that "these ten times have ye reproached me" at ch. 19:3; and, far from yielding an inch, he assumes his old position and retracts nothing — like many of his complexion in every age, determined to believe his own judgment infallible and that he could not err. He retracts nothing of what he had said, but reoccupies his old ground, as sure of his own rectitude as he is of Job's guilt. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the first clause to "the reproof of my shame," a reproof meant to put him to shame, and renders the second more literally, "out of my understanding my spirit answereth me" — Zophar professing to be moved by an inward impulse he cannot but obey. The whole verse, on his reading, is Zophar's plea that necessity, and not mere choler, forces the answer from him.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the "understanding" at its word, glossing the verse as Zophar's disclaimer: "I speak not from passion, but from certain knowledge." Yet that very disclaimer is where the debate turns. Gill's two readings mark the poles — either Zophar answers from a stung and impatient spirit that could not endure Job's check, or he answers as one who believes himself the mouthpiece of a divine correction. Clarke and Ellicott hear chiefly the impulse of an offended man; Wesley lets stand the claim to reasoned knowledge. The witnesses converge only on the irony the reader is meant to feel, that a man so sure his understanding informs him should prove, in the sequel, to understand Job's case so little.
4:
With his temper vented, Zophar reaches back to what he takes for a settled and universal maxim, appealing to a knowledge as old as the race itself. The reformed John Gill renders "of old" as "from eternity," from the beginning of time and the foundation of the world: this, Zophar implies, is no novelty of his own but an ancient and established truth, confirmed by numberless instances ever since men were. Gill is careful that Job could not literally have known it "of old," being of yesterday; the meaning is that the doctrine to be delivered is a maxim of long standing, which the knowing man Zophar takes Job to be must surely own.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the second clause literally — "since Adam was placed on the earth" — and reads the whole as a maxim as ancient as the world, that a wicked man may triumph but a short time before God destroys the proud doer. He cannot resist a thrust at Job, who had lately spoken with such confidence of a general judgment: such is thy character, Clarke has Zophar insinuate, that thou hast little reason to anticipate that day with joy. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the appeal, "knowest thou this which is from everlasting, since man was placed upon the earth," setting it as the solemn preface to the thesis of the next verse.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds how the doctrine is introduced — as an appeal at once to Job's own conviction and to the experience of all ages. "Knowest thou not this? Canst thou be ignorant of a truth so plain?" Those know little, Henry says, who do not know that the wages of sin is death; ever since man was made he has had this truth written in his heart, that the sin of sinners will be their ruin, and ever since there were instances of wickedness there were instances of its punishment, from the expulsions of Adam and Cain onward. When sin entered the world, death entered with it, and all the world knows that "vengeance suffereth not to live" (Acts 28:4), and subscribes to the woe of Isaiah 3:11, that it shall be ill with the wicked. The witnesses do not divide over the maxim; they only let the reader see the flaw in Zophar's use of it, that a truth confessed by all mankind is here made the instrument of condemning a man to whom it does not apply.
5:
"The triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment" — with this the thesis of the whole speech is laid down, and the witnesses mark how far Zophar's party has been driven to admit it. The reformed John Gill recalls that at the first the friends would scarcely own that the wicked prosper at all; beaten from that ground, they now grant that a wicked man may flourish, but insist it is only for a little while. The Hebrew, Gill notes, sets the triumph "from near": it began, as it were, but lately, and, as the Targum paraphrases, it will be quickly ended. The concession is real, but it is fenced with a limit meant to catch Job in its net.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the burden plainly: Zophar affirms that the destruction of the wicked is not only certain but speedy, and he compares the fleeting life of man swept away in Ps. 103:16 and the vanishing of ch. 7:8. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet, "that the triumphing of the evil-doer is not long, and the joy of the godless is but for a moment," so that the two clauses are one measured verdict upon a prosperity Zophar allows only that he may pronounce it brief. The wicked man's glory, on this showing, is a thing already half-gone in the very moment it is seen.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the word "hypocrite," for it is as a hypocrite that Zophar means Job. Zophar asserts the misery not only of those openly wicked and profane, but of hypocrites, who practise wickedness secretly under a show of religion; and it is true, Henry grants, that a form of godliness made a cloak for maliciousness does but make bad worse — dissembled piety is double iniquity, and its ruin will be accordingly, for "the hottest place in hell will be the portion of hypocrites," as our Saviour intimates at Matt. 24:51. Yet Henry grants what Zophar grants, that wicked men may for a time be secure, and easy, and merry, triumphing in their wealth and power over their honest neighbours. Job's friends, Henry recalls, were at the first loth to own that wicked men prosper at all, until Job proved it plainly; and now Zophar yields the point, only to fence it with the limit that such prosperity cannot last. The witnesses do not divide on the truth of the maxim; they divide, silently, from its author, who lays down a sound doctrine only to aim it, unjustly, at a sufferer whose joy was gone and whose piety was no pretence.
6:
Having pronounced the triumph brief, Zophar now paints it at its imagined height, that the fall may be the more dreadful. The reformed John Gill fills in the picture from Scripture's own giants of pride: though the wicked man's excellency mount up to the heavens, as the Assyrian monarch aspired to ascend into heaven and exalt his throne above the stars of God in Isaiah 14:13, or as the great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom whose height reached unto heaven in Daniel 4:11 — yet the loftier the rise, the more appalling the ruin that Zophar is preparing to describe. The loftier images — the heaven, the stars, the towering tree — are chosen, Gill implies, precisely that their overthrow may be the more complete.

The wesleyan-arminian voices take the verse two ways. Adam Clarke, keeping to his reading of the chapter as an allegory of the Fall, refers the "excellency" back to the original state of Adam, created in the image of God and mounting, as it were, to heaven, but by his sin cast down into wretchedness, misery, death, and destruction — so that the wicked man's greatness only re-enacts a ruin as old as Eden. John Wesley keeps it in the plain present: though the man be "advanced to great dignity and authority," his height is no security. The two Arminian readings do not so much contend as run on parallel lines, the one tracing the pride to its archetype, the other content with the man before him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supposes the prosperity as high as imagination can reach. It is not the man's wisdom or virtue but his worldly wealth and greatness that he accounts his excellency and values himself upon; we may suppose it to mount up to the heavens, and, since his spirit always rises with his condition, his head to reach the clouds. He is every way advanced; the world has done its utmost for him; he looks down upon all about him with disdain while they look up with admiration, envy, or fear; we may even suppose him to bid fair for a universal monarchy, and to think himself as far out of the reach of his enemies' darts as if he were in the clouds. His pride and security, Henry adds, are but the certain presages of the misery to come, the height itself the measure of the fall. The witnesses do not divide; they let Zophar build his tower of prosperity to its full height, knowing that the whole force of his argument lies in the suddenness with which, in the verses to come, he will bring it down.
7:
"Yet he shall perish for ever like his own dung" — the sentence is the harshest image Zophar has yet coined, and the witnesses handle both its coarseness and the doctrine hidden under it. The reformed John Gill spreads the ruin over both worlds: the wicked man shall perish not only in his outward substance here and his body in the grave, but in his soul to all eternity, and that in the most shameful manner, perishing in his own corruption as inevitably as dung is never gathered back to its place. He recalls that the ancients reckoned dead bodies as dung, and that the Arabians were said to bury even their kings in dunghills, so loathsome to God and good men does the proud oppressor become. He perishes, Gill says, in his own corruption, and like his own dung is never returned to its place, cast out of the world as a thing men are glad to be rid of.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the same words a colder note, and a covert denial. Zophar, he suggests, here hints his disbelief in the very doctrine of the resurrection that Job had so solemnly asserted in the preceding chapter: the wicked man is dust, and to dust he shall return, his flesh rotting in the earth with no rising promised; and Clarke calls the sentence "a speech that partakes as much of the malevolence as of the asperity of Zophar's spirit." His reputation shall be as abominable as his putrid carcase resembling his own excrement.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the graduated terror of the fall. It shall be a shameful destruction, the man perishing "like his own dung," a thing the world is glad to be rid of, as at Isaiah 66:24; a surprising destruction, brought to desolation in a moment, so that those who saw him but now shall ask "Where is he?" as at Ps. 73:19; and, as the following verses will say, a swift, an utter, and a final ruin. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, simply carry the whole run of verses forward in their rendering, joining "they which have seen him shall say, Where is he?" to the vanishing dream that follows. The abruptness of the question, they note, measures the completeness of the disappearance: he who filled every eye is on a sudden nowhere to be found. The witnesses do not divide over the doom; Clarke alone hears beneath it Zophar's quiet refusal of the hope Job had just confessed, that though worms destroy the body, yet in his flesh he should see God.
8:
The image shifts from the dunghill to the dream, and the witnesses follow Zophar as he makes the great man's whole substance dissolve into nothing. The reformed John Gill offers two ways of taking "he shall fly away as a dream." It may be as a dream forgotten, like the vision that fled from Nebuchadnezzar and could not be recalled; or, better, as the very stuff of a dream, which even when remembered is mere illusion — as a hungry man dreams he eats and a thirsty man that he drinks, but, awaking, finds himself empty and unrefreshed, the fancied banquet fled and never having had any being but in his imagination, the picture drawn in Isaiah 29:8. So the man's whole estate, for all its show, had no more substance than the meal a dreamer thinks he eats.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse, as he reads much of the chapter, with one eye on Job's confession of the resurrection. Instead of rising again from corruption with a new body, as Job had asserted at ch. 19:26, the wicked man's flesh shall rot in the earth and his spirit be dissipated like a vapour; and, like a vision of the night, nothing shall remain of him but the bare impression that such a creature once existed, which shall appear no more for ever. The polemic edge is unmistakable: what Job hoped would be raised, Zophar consigns to a mist that the morning burns off.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his catalogue of the ruin's qualities. It is a swift destruction — the man shall fly away upon the wings of his own terrors, chased away by the just imprecations of all about him, who would gladly be rid of him; and it is an utter destruction, for he shall go away like a dream or a vision of the night, a mere phantasm, so that whatever in it pleased the fancy is quite gone, and nothing remains but matter for others to laugh at the folly of. What charmed the fancy while the vision lasted leaves, when it breaks, only the folly of having trusted it. The witnesses do not divide; together they let Zophar reduce the towering prosperity of the last verse to the substance of a dream, real enough while it lasts and worth nothing when the sleeper wakes — a true word about the world's goods, and a cruel one on the lips of a man using it to bury the hope of a brother.
9:
Zophar completes the vanishing with a line on the emptiness the great man leaves behind, and the witnesses, few here, dwell on the desolation of the place that knew him. The reformed John Gill weighs which of two senses the words carry. "The eye also which saw him shall see him no more" may mean the eye shall no longer behold him busy and concerned in the affairs of life, and especially in the grandeur he once wore; but the parallel that follows, Gill judges, makes the plainer sense the better, that death has taken him quite away, so that neither the admiring eye nor his own familiar place shall behold him any more. The words carry, Gill allows, a double loss — of the man's public greatness, and of the man himself — and the second, being the plainer, he takes for the truer.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the verse its full note of finality. This is a final ruin, Henry says: the eye that saw him — and was ready, in the days of his height, to adore him — shall see him no more, and the place he filled shall no more behold him, having given him an eternal farewell when he went to his own place, as it is written of Judas that he "went to his own place" at Acts 1:25. The very personification of the place that "shall no more behold him" turns the man's absence into a kind of universal forgetting, as though the ground itself refused to remember him.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, keep the couplet in its bare force in their rendering — "the eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him" — the second half echoing and sealing the first, the place itself made a personified witness to his absence. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the last stroke in Zophar's portrait of the wicked man's disappearance, the admiring eye and the accustomed place alike emptied of him. It is, once more, a true observation of how the world closes over the departed and how soon the honoured are forgotten; but the reader, watching Zophar bend every such truth toward the ruin of an innocent man, feels the chill of a doctrine correct in itself and merciless in its intent, spoken over one whose place at home had indeed been emptied — not by his wickedness, but by the hand of God trying his servant.
10:
From the wicked man's vanishing Zophar turns to the reckoning that overtakes his house, and the verse itself is disputed among the witnesses. The reformed John Gill reads it of the children left behind: often visited in wrath for their fathers' sins, they "shall seek to please the poor" — to court the goodwill of those their father had oppressed, that these may not reproach them, take revenge, or seek the law against them — while "his hands shall restore their goods," the plunder disgorged. Yet Gill notes that Jarchi and others turn the clause quite otherwise, so that the meaning is far from settled.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses a reading of sheer reversal. The children shall be reduced to the lowest degree of poverty and want, obliged to become servants to the very poor — the abjectest state conceivable, as when it was said "a servant of servants shall he be" over Ham in Genesis 9:25; and "his hands shall restore their goods" means the wealth wrung from others must be given back. He records too Good's rendering, "his branches shall be involved in his iniquity," and Calmet's, that "his own hands shall render to himself the evil he did to others" — confessing that the clause is variously translated. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers both poles in a breath: the children "shall seek the favour" of the poor by making good what had been taken, or else, read the other way, "the poor shall oppress his children." So the debate is real — whether the verse foretells the sons appeasing their father's victims, or the sons sunk into servitude, or the poor turning at last upon the oppressor's seed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, here beginning the long anatomy of the wicked man's sin and punishment that runs to the chapter's end, sets the verse under the head of forced restitution. So loud shall be the clamour of the poor whom he has impoverished that he shall be constrained to send his children to soothe them and beg their pardon, while his own hands restore what he seized — not with the joy of a Zacchaeus, who gave back fourfold and had much left over at Luke 19:8, but with the pain of a vomit, wrung from him by a despairing conscience. The witnesses do not resolve the grammar; they agree that Zophar means the man's ill-got estate to flow back out of his family as fast as it flowed in, and that the whole is aimed, cruelly, at a Job who had truly lost his children and his goods.
11:
Zophar reaches now for the body itself, and finds the wicked man's very bones freighted with his early sins; the witnesses divide over what the Hebrew charges them with. The reformed John Gill takes it morally: man is a transgressor from the womb, and youth is addicted to pride, passion, lust, luxury, intemperance, and uncleanness, the effects of which are seen long after in bodily disease, the rottenness and consumption of the flesh and the very putrefaction of the bones; though he allows that some read the word of "secret sins," which, unrepented, God will yet find out and bring into judgment.

The wesleyan-arminian voices split the difference. Adam Clarke reports that our version follows the Vulgate, "his bones shall be filled with the sins of his youth," while the Syriac, Arabic, and Targum read "his bones are full of marrow"; but he leans, with Rosenmuller and Good, to taking the Hebrew as "his hidden things," so that it is the man's secret vices that bring down his strength to the dust. John Wesley keeps it simplest of all: "bones" stand for the whole body, even its strongest parts, and "the sin" means the punishment of it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a third sense, rendering the word "his youth" or "youthful vigour," as at ch. 33:25 and Ps. 89:46: though the man be in the full vigour of life, yet that vigour "shall lie down with him in the dust." So three readings stand side by side — the sins of youth, the hidden vices, and the vigour of youth cut short.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unites the moral and the physical. The lusts of the flesh are here called the sins of his youth, the sins that age is most tempted to; and the man's bones are "full of them" in that by drunkenness, gluttony, and wantonness when young he contracted the diseases that gnaw him long after and, as Solomon warns, "consume his flesh and his body" at Prov. 5:11. These he carries to the grave, so that the sins of his youth lie down with him in the dust and his iniquity is upon his bones there, as at Ezekiel 32:27 — the sin of sinners following them to the other side of death. The witnesses do not finally divide over the pathos; they part only over the philology, whether the bones are full of guilt, of secret vice, or of a youthful strength doomed to rot.
12:
Now Zophar draws his most elaborate figure — sin held in the mouth as a delicious morsel — and the witnesses attend both to what the sweetness signifies and to whom the picture is aimed. The reformed John Gill inclines to read the "wickedness" that is sweet as the sin of covetousness, the getting of riches by unlawful means, which Broughton renders "wrong"; though it will bear the wider sense of sin in general, which is sweet to the unregenerate man who savours the things of the flesh, whose taste is unchanged, who drinks iniquity like water and commits sin with greediness. Sin is natural to such a man, Gill adds, who is conceived, born, and brought up in it, and calls bitter sweet and sweet bitter.

The wesleyan-arminian voices develop the allegory. Adam Clarke reads the next several verses as one sustained figure: the man takes what is in truth poison, and is so delighted with its sweetness that he rolls it under his tongue and will scarcely let it down, sparing it, forsaking it not, keeping it still within his mouth — until, swallowed, it turns to the gall of asps within him. The man cannot bear to let the sweet thing down quickly, but keeps it under his tongue, so loath is he to lose the taste. John Wesley pictures the epicure with his sweet morsel, which he keeps and rolls about his mouth that he may the longer enjoy the pleasure of it. The imagery is vivid, and the witnesses feel its edge.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns that edge back upon the speaker. Zophar, he says, draws his wicked man after the pattern of a gourmand or glutton; and if this was meant to apply to Job, it was a fresh instance of heartless cruelty, as well as of an entire want of discernment of character and of unfitness for the office of judge Zophar was so ready to assume. It is possible, Ellicott adds, that the reproach aimed at Job was that of an inordinate love of riches, which Zophar extracted from the bare fact that Job had been a wealthy man — as though prosperity itself were proof of the crime. The witnesses do not divide over the force of the figure; they let Ellicott register the injustice of it, that a portrait of secret greed and cherished sin should be painted for the accusing of a man whose losses had stripped him of everything he owned. Zophar, unable to read the character before him, mistakes a stripped and suffering saint for a secret glutton of forbidden pleasure.
13:
The morsel is held and savoured, and the witnesses linger on the tenderness with which the wicked man cherishes his sin. The reformed John Gill fixes on "though he spare it": it is not that he feeds sparingly, for he eats freely and with greediness, but that he will not spit it out as loathsome; he retains it as sweet and pleasant, sparing it as Saul spared Agag, and as a man spares his only son, since the sin is a darling, a very child of his heart, and therefore dear to him. The keeping of it "still within his mouth" is the tenacity of a man who will not part with his pleasure; he rolls the sin as a dainty morsel, unwilling to let so sweet a thing go down and be done with.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, carry the figure forward in their rendering, "he carefully cherished it and did not let it go, and retained it in his palate," and they note how the coming reversal answers the classical dream of a golden age, when, as the poets sang, rivers of milk and rivers of nectar flowed — the very abundance that Zophar will presently turn to poison and gall. The learned allusion sets the sweetness of the mouth against the bitterness of the belly that is to come.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the moral of the held morsel two ways. To keep the sin still in his mouth denotes the man's obstinate persistence: he spares it when he should kill and mortify it, and forsakes it not, but holds it fast and goes on frowardly; or it denotes his re-acting of the sin by revolving it and remembering it with pleasure, as that adulterous woman multiplied her whoredoms by calling to remembrance the days of her youth in Ezekiel 23:19. Or again, to hide it under the tongue may denote the hypocrite's industrious concealment of his beloved lust, keeping his haunts of sin secret to save the credit of his profession — yet He who knows the heart knows also what is under the tongue, and will discover it shortly. Whether the figure paints obstinate persistence, or the fond remembrance of past sin, or the hypocrite's careful concealment, all three, Henry says, are but ways of loving a sin too well to let it go. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar is describing a sin loved, guarded, and hidden, and that the loving guard of it is the very thing that will make its aftertaste so bitter.
14:
The sweetness now turns in the swallowing, and the witnesses trace the moment the cherished morsel becomes venom in the belly. The reformed John Gill reads the "meat" as the sin the man lives on and lives in, his bread of deceit: it promises pleasure, profit, and impunity, but proves ashes and gravel-stones; as undigested meat turns in the stomach, or rather the stomach turns against it, so his sin, once so agreeable, distresses and sickens him. The figure marks, Gill notes, the finishing of sin after it has been conceived in the mind and completed in the act. The bread of deceit, sweet in the eating, lies heavy after, and the very stomach that welcomed it turns against it.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the reversal in a phrase: the meat is "turned" from sweet to bitter, into "the gall of asps," than which nothing is more bitter or more pernicious — for gall is most bitter, the gall of serpents full of poison, and the poison of asps most deadly, killing within a few hours without remedy. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the line, "his bread is now changed in his bowels, it is the gall of vipers within him," setting the inward transformation as the hinge of the whole passage. The turn from sweetness to gall, they mark, falls in the belly, where the swallowed morsel does its secret and deadly work.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the change its spiritual reading. The unquietness of the wicked man's mind arises from his conscience: even the wickedness that was sweet in the commission, and rolled under the tongue as a delicate morsel, becomes bitter in the reflection, and, when reviewed, fills him with horror. In his bowels it is turned, Henry says, like the little book of the Revelation that was in the mouth sweet as honey but in the belly bitter, at Rev. 10:10; such a thing is sin, turned into the gall of asps, and so it will prove to him — what he sucked so sweetly becoming his poison, the fawning tongue turning at last into the viper's. All the charming graces that seemed to be in the sin become, when conscience wakes, so many raging furies. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar has caught a real law of guilt, that stolen sweetness sours into gall, and that he presses it, as ever, to make the sick and grieving Job the very man whose feast has turned to poison.
15:
"He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again" — the figure of the poisoned meat is now spoken out as plainly rifled wealth, and the witnesses read the disgorging as the heart of Zophar's threat. The reformed John Gill takes the riches to be not the man's own but another's, spoiled and devoured with as much eagerness as a hungry man swallows his food; his immoderate love of wealth stops at nothing to obtain it, and once it is in his possession he reckons it as safe as meat in his belly, never dreaming of restitution — which yet, Gill says, must come. He swallowed the spoil as safe as meat in his belly, and thought never to refund it; but refund it he must, whether he will or no.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the medical realism of his allegory: the vomiting is the very effect of most ordinary poisons, which occasion a nausea and often excruciating retching, as nature strives to eject what, if retained, would be its bane. As poison stirs the frame to reject it, so the plundered wealth will not stay down. So the ill-gotten wealth acts within the man like venom, and his own frame casts it out. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the whole, "he hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again; God shall cast them out of his belly," so that the disgorging is at once the man's sickness and God's act.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both halves of that single stroke. The wicked man has swallowed riches as greedily as ever a starving man swallowed meat, thinking them now as much his own as the food he has eaten; but he is deceived, for he shall vomit them up again — either his own uneasy conscience shall force him, for the quiet of his mind, to make restitution, and that with the reluctance of a vomit, or, if he will not, "God shall cast them out of his belly" by his providence, bringing it about one way or another that ill-gotten goods return to the right owners, while the love of the sin is not yet cast out of the heart. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar means the plunderer's gains to be torn from him with pain and shame, and that the doctrine — that unjust gain will not stay down — is sound, however unjustly he wields it against a man who had wronged no one.
16:
Zophar names the venom outright, and the witnesses gather round the natural history and the moral of the asp. The reformed John Gill dwells on the creature: its poison lies in the head, particularly in the teeth, a yellow liquor in the gums like oil; he retails Pliny's lurid account of the asps in copulation, and observes that death by the poison of asps was among the ancients a mode of executing malefactors. The point, Gill insists, is not the sweetness of the sin in its commission but the punishment of it — a certain and speedy death, as the venom quickly kills. Death by the asp's poison, Gill notes, was a punishment inflicted on malefactors among some peoples, sure and swift, so that the figure carries its own sentence.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as the pivot of his allegory: that delicious morsel, the secret and easily-besetting sin so palatable and pleasurable, shall act on the life of the soul as the poison of asps acts on the life of the body. He adds the old lore that the venom of serpents was thought to consist in their gall, citing Pliny that no one should marvel the gall is poison, and that the gall of horses too was ranked among the poisons — the ancients holding the poison to be generated in the gall and exuded when the creature is enraged. The sweet sin, on Clarke's reading, works upon the soul as that gall works upon the body — a pleasure that proves a poison.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the natural image to conscience. What the man sucked so sweetly, and with so much pleasure, will prove to him the poison of asps; so will all unlawful gains be. When conscience is awakened, Henry says, the fawning tongue will prove the viper's tongue, and all the charming graces that were thought to be in sin will turn into so many raging furies. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the line, "he sucked in the poison of vipers," matching the sweetness of the earlier verses with the deadly draught that answers it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar has drawn a true and dreadful equation — that the pleasure of sin is a swallowed poison — and that its very truth makes the cruelty sharper, aimed as it is at a man whose only draught had been the cup of undeserved affliction.
17:
The poison bars the man from every good, and Zophar denies him even the sight of the abundance he coveted; the witnesses spread out the imagery of the "brooks of honey and butter." The reformed John Gill hears first the literal want: the venom excites a burning thirst, yet the man shall not so much as see the rivers of water to assuage it, like the rich man who begged in vain for a drop to cool his tongue at Luke 16:24; and beyond that, the honey and butter betoken a plenty of good things he shall never taste.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the fullest gloss, following Good: honey and butter are the natural yield of a rich, well-watered pasturage, and the phrase, plainly proverbial, denotes the highest temporal prosperity. He heaps up the parallels — Job's own washing his steps with butter at ch. 29:6, the land flowing with milk and honey of Exodus 3:8, the butter and honey of Isaiah 7:22, and the hills flowing with milk in Joel 3:18 — and adds that the Greek and Roman poets, Pindar and Virgil and Ovid and Horace, abound in the same figures of streaming honey and milk. The land flowing with milk and honey was, to the Hebrew ear, the very emblem of abundance and blessing, and it is that emblem Zophar denies the wicked man. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps it short: the man shall not "see," that is, not enjoy, the abundant satisfaction which good men through God's blessing enjoy.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the phrase a hint about the age of the book itself. Zophar uses language that might lead one to suppose him familiar with the promise of Canaan; but since the wording is not precisely identical, it may rather show a community of proverbial speech, so that "a land flowing with milk and honey" was an expression already in common use and not one original with the Pentateuch. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the disappointment: the man had promised himself rivers of sensual delight, and shall never see them, for the world is not, to those who love and court it, the thing they fancy — the enjoyment always sinks far below the raised expectation. The wicked man had feasted in hope on rivers of delight, and shall not so much as see them. The witnesses do not divide over the picture of plenty forfeited; Ellicott alone lifts the phrase into the long question of when the book of Job was written.
18:
What the man toiled for he must give back untasted, and the witnesses labour over a verse whose Hebrew they find genuinely knotted. The reformed John Gill takes it plainly of restitution: "that which he laboured for shall he restore," the gain he sweated after being wrung from him again — as the vomiting of the earlier verse had figured, so here it is spoken out.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, insist on the exact syntax: the verse does not say he restores it without swallowing it, but rather, because he gives out again what he has acquired, he has no pleasure in it and may not altogether swallow it down. They reject the attempts that would read "property of his restitution" or "the property of another," holding the line to the sense that the man's labour yields him no enjoyment. The several lines of the verse, they insist, keep their own independence, and are not to be forced into one clause against the poet's manner. The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, allows that the latter part is probably right, but offers a variant — "according to the substance that he hath gotten he shall not rejoice" — confessing the phrase uncertain.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke throws the difficulty open with a rueful "O, how doctors disagree!" He prefers, with the Arabic and Syriac, "he shall return to labour, but he shall not eat" — he shall toil and not be permitted to enjoy the fruit of it; and he reports Good's rendering, that leans on Arabic roots for "eat" and for "a barren year," so that God sends dearth on the man's land as his recompense, and Houbigant's, "he shall restore what he gained by labour, nor shall he consume it." He closes, as often, with old Coverdale's homely turn: "laboure shal he, and yet have nothinge to eate." John Wesley keeps the drift simple — he shall not swallow it so as to hold it, nor possess it long, but be forced to part with his estate to make compensation for his wrongs. He shall not enjoy what he had gotten, Wesley says, because it shall be taken from him. The witnesses do not divide over the substance, that the man's gain profits him nothing; they divide, and freely own it, over the tangled letter of the verse, where honest scholars pull the words half a dozen ways.
19:
"Because he hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor" — Zophar names at last the crime for which all this ruin is the wage, and the witnesses register both the charge and its baselessness against Job. The reformed John Gill reads the clause of a settled cruelty: the man first crushes and breaks the poor to pieces, and then leaves them so, without pity or relief — not that he once helped and afterwards forsook them, but that he does not leave off until he has oppressed them; Broughton's blunter reading, "he oppresseth and leaveth poor," comes to the same. The second clause Gill takes of his seizing "a house which he builded not," the plunder of another's labour; the whole clause, on his reading, paints not a lapse of charity but a fixed and heartless policy of oppression.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the Hebrew a sharper turn: "he hath broken in pieces the forsaken of the poor" — the poor have fled from famine and left their children behind, and this hard-hearted man has suffered the little ones to perish when he might have saved them alive; and he has "thrown down a house and not rebuilt it," destroying a family that, by helping the wretched, he might have preserved from extinction. Clarke does not miss that all this is aimed, "meaning Job all the while," at the very man once famous for his charity, so that the accusation recoils upon the accuser who frames it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott says it outright: for these insinuations there was not a vestige of ground, and Job formally rebuts them in the great apology of chapter 31, where he calls to witness his open door, his care of the fatherless, and the fleece of his sheep that warmed the poor. The witnesses do not divide over the meaning of the verse — that oppression of the helpless is the root sin Zophar lays to the wicked man's account — but they stand together, silently, over the injustice of the charge, for the reader knows, and Zophar does not, that the man before him had been the eyes of the blind and the feet of the lame. Here, more nakedly than anywhere in the speech, Zophar's sound doctrine and his groundless slander are one and the same word, and the witnesses let the gap between the charge and the man speak its own rebuke.
20:
Zophar traces the ruin inward, to a greed that never knows rest, and the witnesses read the verse as the sentence of a soul that can hold nothing. The reformed John Gill sets aside the gentler gloss — that the man shall find no happiness in his children or contentment in his substance, ever craving more — and takes the words rather as punishment: he "shall not feel quietness in his belly," shall have no peace of mind nor quiet in his conscience, because of the unlawful way in which his riches were got. The restless craving that was his sin becomes the sleeplessness that is his plague; this inward unrest, Gill insists, is the punishment written into the very sin.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the insatiability. Adam Clarke, remarking that the Hebrew word for "belly" often means the whole trunk of a man, with all the thoughts and inclinations seated there, reads the verse as an endless, unsatisfied desire after secular good, which the man shall never be able to fill. So the punishment is fitted to the sin: a bottomless appetite is given nothing that can quiet it. John Wesley keeps it close: "he shall have no peace in his mind," and "he shall not save," that is, not keep, any part of his desirable things, but shall forfeit and lose them all.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two dreads of the wicked man's mind, looking back and looking forward. The ill-gotten wealth he swallowed makes him sick, and, like undigested meat, is always upbraiding him; he "shall not feel quietness in his belly," having not that ease in his own mind which people think he has, but a continual agitation. He is disquieted looking back, by a conscience full of the fear of God's wrath, and looking forward, by cares that will not let him rest. Let none, Henry warns, expect to enjoy comfortably what they have gotten unjustly. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar here names a real and inward misery — that the covetous heart, having no rest in itself, can find rest in nothing it grasps — and that he sets it, as he sets all, to the account of a man whose disquiet was not the gnawing of guilt but the wound of a mysterious affliction. The doctrine is sound, that a greedy heart carries its own unrest and finds in its gains no peace; the aim of it, once more, falls wide of the patient man it was meant to strike.
21:
Because his craving spared nothing, nothing shall be spared to him, and the witnesses take the verse as the exact match of the man's greed and his loss. The reformed John Gill reads "there shall none of his meat be left" first of the poison disgorged — none of it left in his belly, all cast up — and then of his substance, none of it left for himself, his children, or his heirs, all consumed; so ravenous had been the getting that nothing remains of the estate. He notes a second turn some give the words, "there shall be none left for his meat," that is, no heir to inherit it, his family cut off. The insatiable devouring leaves nothing behind — nothing in the belly, nothing in the estate, nothing for the heirs.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the greed and the desolation. Adam Clarke gives old Coverdale's rendering, "he devoured so gredily that he left nothinge behynde, therefore his goodes shal not prospere," and adds that the man shall be stripped of everything. John Wesley reads the closing "therefore" of the sequel: it being publicly known that the man was totally ruined, none of his kindred shall trouble themselves about any relics of his estate, none expecting to be a penny the better for him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the verse to the same effect but points the moral in its logic — "there was nothing left that he devoured not, therefore his prosperity shall not endure" — so that the very completeness of his devouring is the reason his good things cannot last. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry joins the picture to the man's isolation: when he is dead, no man shall look for his goods, nor any relation be willing to take out letters of administration for what he leaves. His neighbours and kindred reckon him so utterly ruined that not one of them expects to be a penny the better for him. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar means the insatiable getter to end with nothing and no one — the estate consumed, the heirs cut off, the very kindred indifferent — and that the sentence, true of many a grasping life, is levelled once more at a man whose losses were the trial of his faith and not the wages of his greed. What Zophar paints as the end of rapacity is, in Job, the innocent stripping of a servant God was proving.
22:
At the very peak of his plenty the blow falls, and the witnesses savour the paradox Zophar has caught in a phrase — abundance itself turned to distress. The reformed John Gill unfolds it: though the man have a fulness of temporal blessings, as much as heart can wish or more, yet amidst it all he shall be reduced to the utmost straits — whether through fear of losing what he has, so that his abundance will not let him sleep; or through a narrowness of spirit that cannot enjoy the fruit of his labours; or through dread of coming want; or, likeliest, by being suddenly dispossessed of all, as Nebuchadnezzar was, in the very height of his prosperity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls the line "a fine saying," which few menders of Job's text have improved: it is literally true of every great, rich, wicked man, who, having no God, is tormented by anxieties and perplexities though his portion be in this life; and "every hand of the wicked shall come upon him" means all kinds of misery for his portion. John Wesley reads the second clause of retribution in kind — his wickedness punished "by those as wicked as himself."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott parts company on that clause. He renders it, "the hand of every one that is in misery shall come upon him," taking the assailants to be the wretched whom the man had wronged, now turning upon him in retaliation — or, less probably, every blow that can render a man miserable. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, carry the sentence straight into the next: in order to fill his insatiable belly, God will send forth against him the glowing fury of His wrath and rain it into his very flesh, and they hear in the phrase an echo of the doom of Zephaniah 1:17. So a small difference runs beneath the agreement — whether the "hand" that falls is the wicked at large, or the miserable he oppressed, or the immediate hand of God — while the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the inward reading, that in the fulness of his sufficiency the man is in straits through the anxieties of his own mind, like the rich fool crying "What shall I do?" at Luke 12:17. The witnesses do not divide over the paradox; they only weigh whose hand it is that spoils the feast.
23:
The stroke is timed, with terrible precision, to the moment of the feast, and the witnesses feel the weight of "while he is eating." The reformed John Gill reads "when he is about to fill his belly" both ways — of the man sitting down to an ordinary meal to satisfy nature, and of his figuratively seeking to gorge his barns and coffers and find satisfaction in his increase — just as the wrath is poised to strike.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds every word here speaking terror. It is not only the justice of God that is engaged against the man but his wrath, the deep resentment of provocations given to himself; it is the fury of his wrath, incensed to the highest; it is cast upon him with force and rained upon him in abundance, coming on his head like the fire and brimstone upon Sodom, to which the psalmist points at Ps. 11:6 — and against this, Henry says, there is no fence but in Christ, the only covert from the storm and tempest of Isaiah 32:2. The wrath falls when the man is about to glut himself, secure and easy, as the ruin of the old world and of Sodom came in the depth of their security, as our Lord observes at Luke 17:26; and here, Henry notes with a shudder, "perhaps Zophar here reflects on the death of Job's children when they were eating and drinking," recalling the feast at which the house fell in ch. 1:18.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears instead a plain allusion to Israel's lustings in the desert, when God rained down quails and rained his wrath while the flesh was yet in their mouths at Numbers 11:33; he even reads the "quietness" of the earlier verse as the quail itself, and lays the whole passage beside the murmurings and plagues of the wilderness. John Wesley marks the double force of "rain": it names both the Author of the plagues, God, and their nature, that they shall come with a vehemence the man cannot avoid — and the pointed "eating," he adds, is "as it fell upon thy sons." Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, confirm the grammar of the sudden sending-forth of wrath. The witnesses do not divide over the terror; two of them hear in Zophar's timing a barb aimed straight at the wound of Job's bereavement.
24:
Flight is now cut off, and the witnesses follow the man from one weapon into the reach of another. The reformed John Gill reads "he shall flee from the iron weapon" of the sword — the flaming sword of God's justice, which fleeing betrays a guilty and terrified conscience; yet there is no escaping the hand of God nor fleeing from his presence, so that the flight is vain. The very act of fleeing, Gill observes, argues a guilty and frightened conscience; yet flee where he will, he cannot outrun the hand that pursues him.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, set the two clauses as a conditional pair: if he flee from the weapons of iron, the deadly arms in the thick of the fight, he yet succumbs to what is destructive by and by — "the bow of brass shall pierce him through." The flight of the disheartened is itself a punishment, completed by the arrow that the brazen bow sends after him with swift power, striking him as he runs. The doom is doubled: escape from the near weapon only delivers him to the far. The disheartened man's flight is itself a stroke of the judgment, the arrow of the brazen bow completing what the iron weapon had begun.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way — "though he should flee from the iron armour, the brazen bow should strike him through" — and gives Coverdale's version, "so that yf he fle the yron weapens, he shal be shott with the stele bow," concluding that all kinds of death await him, and he shall most certainly perish; whichever weapon he escapes, another stands ready. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the principle in a line: "if he escaped one mischance, another should overtake him." The witnesses do not divide; together they hear Zophar deny the wicked man every exit, so that the sword he dodges only hands him to the bow, and no single deliverance avails a man the whole armoury of heaven is bent against. It is a true word about the inescapability of judgment when God is the pursuer, and, on Zophar's lips, one more arrow aimed at a man already, as he thought, marked out for destruction — though the reader knows the mark upon Job was set by another hand and for another end. The truth of the doom is not in question; only its address, which lights on the one man in the story it does not fit.
25:
The arrow that struck him is drawn out, and with it the man's life; the witnesses read the verse as the death-agony of Zophar's wicked man. The reformed John Gill takes it of the shaft withdrawn from the body — drawn out, it may be, that the wound might be healed, but to no purpose, since the hurt is mortal; the terrors that follow are the terrors of death, for the man perceives his wound incurable. Whether drawn out by his own hand or another's, the shaft comes forth too late, and the horror upon him is the horror of a death he knows he cannot escape.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, carry the run of verses in their rendering — "it is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him" — and read the "glittering sword" of the flashing arrow-head or blade wrenched from the vitals, so that the bright steel comes forth from the very seat of life. The blade drawn from the gall, they and Wesley agree, marks a wound as deep as it is deadly. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the archery: the arrow is drawn from the sheaf, discharged from the bow, and passes through the body, as Coverdale has it, "the arowe shal be taken forth, and go out at his backe." John Wesley fixes the anatomy — the shaft that had entered is now drawn out of the gall, which shows the wound both deep and deadly, and the "terrors" are the terrors of a death he knows to be past cure. The gall, Wesley notes, is named on purpose, to fix the very seat of the mortal hurt.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the close, "yea, terrors overtake him," and adds the note the witnesses cannot forget: even when the man has escaped a second and a third calamity, terrors shall still be upon him — "this was all perfectly true in a sense, yea, even a truism, but it was utterly false in its application to Job himself." The witnesses do not divide over the picture of a mortal wound and its horrors; Ellicott names for them the whole tragedy of the speech, that a description true of the impenitent is being turned, falsely, into the sentence of a righteous man. The wound is real, and the terror real, but the man they are laid upon is guiltless.
26:
"A fire not blown shall consume him" — the doom deepens into darkness and a supernatural flame, and the witnesses weigh both the hidden darkness and the fire no human hand has kindled. The reformed John Gill reads "all darkness shall be hid in his secret places" of calamity laid up for the man in the very places where he promised himself safety: utter darkness, the blackness of everlasting wrath, is reserved and treasured among God's stores of vengeance to be brought forth in due time; or, as some take it, all this comes upon him "for his store," that is, for the hoard of his secret sins, which shall be brought into judgment and the hidden things of darkness laid bare.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke catalogues the instruments of ruin Zophar has been naming — the wrath of God, the iron weapon, the bow and arrow, the darkness of horror — and takes "a fire not blown" for a supernatural fire, lightning such as fell in judgment, with a probable allusion to the fire that consumed Korah's company, so that "it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle," as the households of the rebels perished in Numbers 16:32. John Wesley reads the same: all sorts of miseries, laid up by God and infallibly overtaking the man even in the secret places where he hopes to hide; a fire "not blown by man, but kindled by God himself"; and the curse reaching "him that is left," his family, who inherit his curse as well as his estate.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the fire its quiet dread. It is a ruin that comes insensibly: the darkness is a hidden darkness, all darkness without the least mixture of light, hid in his secret place, where he never retires into his own conscience but finds himself in the dark; and the fire, "a fire not blown," is kindled without noise, a consumption whose effects all see but whose cause none sees, wasting him surely but slowly, as a worm at the root withers the gourd. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render it "a fire that is not blown upon devoureth him," feeding on what is left in his tent. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Zophar's picture of a doom secret, supernatural, and inescapable, closing quietly over the man and his house.
27:
Zophar summons heaven and earth as witnesses against the wicked man, and here the witnesses part gently over who "the heaven" is that reveals his iniquity. The reformed John Gill offers three senses at once: it may be God, who dwells in heaven and knows all things secret as well as open, and will make them manifest; or the angels of heaven, who in the last day shall gather out of the kingdom all that do iniquity, as at Matt. 13:41; or the judgments that descend visibly from heaven — the drowning of the old world, the fire and brimstone on Sodom, the stroke of thunder and lightning — which, falling on a man, proclaim him guilty of a wrath-deserving crime.

The wesleyan-arminian voices ground it in the wilderness again. Adam Clarke hears another allusion to the destruction of Korah: the heaven revealed their iniquity when the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation, and then the earth rose up against them, the ground cleaving asunder and swallowing them alive, as at Numbers 16:31. John Wesley reads that God shall be a swift witness against the man by extraordinary judgments — still, Wesley notes, reflecting on Job's own case and the fire that had fallen from heaven upon him — while all the creatures of earth conspire to destroy him; if the God of heaven and earth be his enemy, neither heaven nor earth will show him any kindness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the two witnesses into one sentence of doom: the God of heaven, who sees all the secret wickedness of the wicked, will let all the world know what a base man he has been, that they may own the justice of God; and the earth shall rise up against him, as the stomach rises against what is loathsome, refusing to keep him, disclosing her blood as at Isaiah 26:21 — heaven revealing his iniquity and refusing to receive him, so that whither can he go but to hell? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sums it and marks the close of the speech: all nature combines to bring about the ruin decreed by God — "and here we take leave of Zophar, who does not reply again; he has exhausted himself." Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet plainly, the heavens revealing his iniquity and the earth rising against him. The witnesses do not divide over the sentence; they only spread the meanings of "heaven" between God, his angels, and his visible judgments.
28:
The curse runs on past the man to his house and his goods, and the witnesses read the verse as the sweeping-away of all he leaves behind. The reformed John Gill takes "the increase of his house" for either his children or his substance; and, since the next words speak of flowing away, he records Kimchi's turn that it means the very walls of his house — the stones falling down, the dwelling dilapidated, a ruin expressed by a "flow," as when a downpour of stones is spoken of elsewhere. Either way the household is dissolved.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep to the wilderness parallel and the plain sense. Adam Clarke hears a further allusion to the punishment of Korah's company, whose houses and goods perished with them at Numbers 16:32, holding it more than probable that Zophar knew and quoted the very circumstances. The houses and goods of the rebels perished with them, and Zophar, Clarke thinks, had that judgment plainly in view. John Wesley glosses each phrase: the increase of his house is his estate; "depart" means it shall be lost; "flow" means it shall go like waters, swiftly and strongly and so as to return no more; and the "wrath" is the wrath of God, in whose day of reckoning it is carried off. The flowing away is final, Wesley notes: like waters, the estate departs so as to return no more.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as ruin to the man's family and fortune together. His posterity shall be rooted out: the increase of his house shall depart, cut off by untimely deaths or forced to flee their country; numerous and growing families, if wicked, are soon reduced, dispersed, and extirpated by the judgments of God. And his estate shall sink, his goods flowing away from his family as fast as ever they flowed into it, in the day of God's wrath — for which, all the while his estate was gathering by fraud and oppression, he was in truth treasuring up wrath. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render it, "the produce of his house must vanish, flowing away in the day of God's wrath." The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Zophar means the oppressor's line and living to be swept off together, the gains of injustice draining away in the day they were, unknowingly, laid up to meet. House and fortune go down together, and the treasure of wrath is paid out at last.
29:
"This is the portion of a wicked man from God" — Zophar rounds off his speech like an orator pronouncing sentence, and the witnesses weigh both the finality of the verdict and the flaw in its aim. The reformed John Gill draws the contrast that the word "portion" invites: the good man's portion is God himself, both here and hereafter, but the wicked man's portion, though it too is assigned him from God, is at most a worldly one confined to this life, and hereafter an abode with devils and damned spirits, banished from the presence of God to all eternity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the closing verse as the occasion for a long reflection, holding that Zophar deals with the man as God dealt with the murmuring Israelites and the rebellious sons of Korah — and here Clarke follows the bishop of Killala in reading the earlier "quail" and the rained wrath as pointing to the transgression at Kibroth-hattaavah in Numbers 11:33, an allusion that, if genuine, would fix the poem later than that history and tell against the extreme antiquity so often claimed for the book of Job. John Wesley notes the force of "the heritage," so called to mark its stability and assurance, as firm as an inheritance to the right heir, and set in pointed opposition to the inheritance the wicked man had gotten by fraud and violence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his exposition, both honours the doctrine and exposes its misuse. Zophar concludes that this is the portion allotted, designed, and settled for the wicked man, the heritage of God's decree, of which fair warning is given — "O wicked man, thou shalt surely die," as at Ezekiel 33:8. Yet impenitent sinners, Henry adds, do not always fall under such temporal judgments as Zophar describes, "and therein Zophar was mistaken," though the wrath of God abides on them in spiritual judgments far worse. Never, Henry says, was any doctrine better explained, or worse applied, than this by Zophar, who meant all of it to prove Job a hypocrite; let us receive the good explanation and make the better application, to stand in awe and sin not. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the summary, "this is the lot of the wicked man from Elohim, and the heritage decreed for him from God." The witnesses do not finally divide; they take the verse as a true verdict on impenitence, spoiled by a false address, and let Henry name the whole tragedy of the speech in a phrase.
